author: Philip K. Dick
date_display: Fantasy and Science Fiction, September 1987 (written earlier, unpublished in Dick's lifetime)
card_summary: Cadbury, a discontented beaver in an anthropomorphic animal society run on a poker-chip currency, is nagged by his shrewish wife Hilda into psychiatric treatment with the amiably useless Dr. Drat.
page_summary:
Cadbury, a discontented beaver in an anthropomorphic animal society run on a poker-chip currency, is nagged by his shrewish wife Hilda into psychiatric treatment with the amiably useless Dr. Drat. When a perfumed love letter arrives from a mysterious 'Jane Feckless Foundfully,' Cadbury eagerly answers it, only for Hilda to reveal she wrote the fake letter herself as a loyalty test. Undeterred, Cadbury begins a secret, snuff-tin correspondence floated down the creek with a real woman, Carol Stickyfoot, a psychiatric patient of Dr. Drat's fresh from a breakdown in Madrid, and paddles off to meet her in person. Their meeting escalates through countercultural banter about Zen and blue poker chips before Stickyfoot, in a startling final transformation, splits into three simultaneous women — a cool, analytical companion; a warm, eternally forgiving mother-figure; and a demanding, resentful future-daughter figure — each embodying a different register of relationship Cadbury has sought throughout the story. All three, revealed to want nothing from him but his 'blue chips,' begin to fade him into insubstantiality as they discuss him with increasing indifference, until he dissolves into a wisp of smoke, leaving only the warmest of the three to murmur a private, unheard 'I love you' as the group departs for the beach without him.

**Why it matters.** The story is formally unusual within Dick's corpus for combining a children's-fable premise (a beaver protagonist, anthropomorphic animal society, a folkloric title) with adult countercultural material (explicit language, drug references, Zen Buddhism, psychiatric case histories) and a genuinely disorienting, non-naturalistic climax. Its closest thematic kin in his broader work is the recurring 'trinity of women' pattern later analyzed by critics (Palmer, citing Kim Stanley Robinson and Fredric Jameson) across Dick's novels — the cool analytical figure, the warm eternal mother, and the demanding, resentful dependent all appear, in variously named forms, throughout his fiction. Here that pattern is made unusually explicit and literal: rather than three separate characters across a narrative, they are presented as three simultaneous emanations of a single woman, directly confronting the protagonist with the impossibility of having all the forms of love and relation he wants at once. Cadbury's dissolution into 'a wisp of gray smoke' is presented ambiguously as failure, mercy, and inevitability all at once.

*The cherishing figure's final, private 'I love you,' spoken to herself after Cadbury has already faded into nonexistence and cannot hear it, closes the story on an image of love arriving permanently too late, offered to an absence rather than a presence.*

structure.form: short story in three movements: the failing marriage and psychiatric non-help, the escalating correspondence with a possibly-imaginary woman, and a surreal final transformation and dissolution
movements: Cadbury's marriage to the domineering Hilda and his fruitless psychiatric sessions with Dr. Drat establish his central emptiness, figured as a lifelong craving for rare 'blue chips.'

A fake love letter (revealed as Hilda's loyalty test) is followed by a real, escalating snuff-tin correspondence with Carol Stickyfoot, a fellow psychiatric patient, culminating in Cadbury abandoning his marriage to meet her.

Their meeting culminates in Stickyfoot splitting into three simultaneous female archetypes, each embodying a different mode of relationship Cadbury has sought, before all three fade him into nonexistence and depart without him.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Cadbury throughout, tracking his escalating hope and self-justification right up to the moment his own perspective, and then his existence, dissolves entirely.
structure.central_device: A single desired woman literalizing into three simultaneous, distinct archetypal relationships (analytical equal, unconditional mother, demanding dependent), each of which the protagonist wants and none of which he can actually sustain, ending in his own narrative erasure rather than any resolution of his longing.

characters.name: Cadbury
characters.note: His entire identity is organized around a lack (the title's 'who lacked') — of blue chips, of love, of a stable sense of self — and the story's ending literalizes this lack by having him fade into nonexistence once the object of his longing multiplies beyond his ability to possess any version of it.

characters.name: Hilda
characters.note: Domineering and manipulative (the fake love-letter test), but also given a moment of blunt honesty ('truth, when pitted against hot air... generally carries the day') that the narration itself endorses rather than undercuts.

characters.name: Dr. Drat
characters.note: His diagnosis that Cadbury suffers from 'illusions' rather than psychosis is delivered with genial uselessness, and his casual, dismissive commentary on his own patient Carol Stickyfoot raises unaddressed ethical questions about his professional conduct.

characters.name: Carol Stickyfoot
characters.role: Cadbury's correspondent and the story's central transformation
characters.note: Introduced as a real woman with her own psychiatric history and Zen-inflected countercultural voice, she is ultimately revealed (or transforms into) three simultaneous archetypal women, none of whom is straightforwardly 'her' — the story never clarifies whether this is metaphor, hallucination, or literal event.

settings.name: Papermill Creek and its surrounding gnawing-grounds
settings.note: An anthropomorphic-animal pastoral setting rendered with a jarring collision of countercultural, late-1960s/1970s American idiom (snuff tins, poker chips, Zen references, profanity) grafted onto a children's-fable premise.

settings.name: Carol Stickyfoot's apartment
settings.note: The site of the story's climactic transformation, an ordinary modest domestic space that becomes the stage for an entirely non-naturalistic dissolution of both character and protagonist.

motifs: A protagonist defined entirely by lack (of currency, of love, of self), whose narrative arc ends in literal erasure rather than fulfillment
Countercultural idiom and profanity deliberately jarring against a fable/children's-story register (talking animals, a beaver protagonist, secret notes floated in tins)
A single desired woman fragmenting into multiple simultaneous, irreconcilable archetypal relationships, each wanted and none sustainable
Blue poker chips functioning throughout as a stand-in for whatever the protagonist believes he lacks, whether love, money, or self-worth
A protagonist's own narrative dissolution treated as merciful relief rather than as tragedy — 'And yet that was good. He could survive that.'

distinctive_terms.label: Creator
distinctive_terms.note: Invoked in Cadbury's own mangled attempt at a Zen koan about pleasing 'the Creator.'

pkd_on_this_work.summary: No commentary by Dick on this specific story was found in this evidence pass.

open_questions: When was this story actually written? It was not published until 1987, after Dick's death; its late-1960s/1970s countercultural idiom suggests composition well before publication, but a precise date was not found in this evidence pass.

Is the three-women climax ever discussed by critics (e.g., Palmer, Robinson, Jameson, all of whom analyze Dick's recurring 'character sets' across his novels) as a uniquely explicit, literalized version of that broader pattern?

Is there a documented reason Dick chose a children's-fable/anthropomorphic-animal frame for such tonally adult material, and are there other examples of this specific combination elsewhere in his corpus?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.
